items.name: Mineral Rights
items.meta: Confused about what your West Virginia mineral rights cover versus surface land, royalty, or leasehold? We explain the estate and confirm yours from the deed.

sections.html:
Owning mineral rights in West Virginia means owning a distinct legal estate, separate from the surface, and what exactly it includes depends on the language in a deed that might be a century old.

Mineral rights, sometimes called the mineral estate, give the owner the right to explore for, develop and produce oil, gas and other minerals beneath a tract of land, along with the right to lease those minerals to an operator and receive bonus and royalty payments in exchange. In West Virginia, the mineral estate is very often severed from the surface estate, meaning one person or family owns the surface while a different owner, sometimes a descendant of a coal or timber company from the early 1900s, owns the minerals underneath.

Confirming exactly what your mineral rights cover starts with the severance deed, and the specific wording in that document controls far more than most owners expect.

sections.title: The full mineral estate versus a carved-out piece of it
sections.html:
A full mineral owner holds the right to lease the minerals, negotiate bonus and royalty terms, and receive whatever share of production the lease specifies. But mineral rights can also be divided further, an owner might sell or reserve just the royalty portion while keeping the executive right to lease, or convey an overriding royalty carved out of a specific lease rather than the underlying minerals themselves. If your family's deed history includes multiple transfers, the specific bundle of rights you hold today may be narrower than 'mineral rights' generally implies.

We read the actual granting language in your deed rather than assuming a title labeled 'mineral deed' conveys the full estate, since the specific reservations and exceptions inside the document control.

sections.title: What formations and depths your rights reach
sections.html:
Older West Virginia severance deeds, particularly those from the coal and timber era, sometimes limit the mineral grant to specific substances or depths rather than the entire mineral column. A deed that severed 'coal' alone is a different asset than one severing 'oil, gas and all other minerals.' For owners in the Marcellus and Utica fairway, this distinction matters directly, since a deed limited to shallow rights may not extend to the deeper shale formations operators are targeting today.

We check this specifically before valuing a tract, because a full mineral estate and a depth-limited or substance-limited interest are priced very differently.

sections.title: Surface owner conflicts and access rights
sections.html: West Virginia law generally gives the mineral estate dominance over the surface estate for purposes of reasonable development, meaning an operator can typically access the surface to drill even without the surface owner's consent, subject to reasonable compensation for damages under the state's oil and gas surface owner protections. If you own minerals but not the surface, this dominant-estate principle is part of what makes your interest valuable to a lessee. If you own both, it's worth understanding how a future lease might affect the surface separately from the royalty income.

sections.title: Confirming your specific rights before a sale
sections.html: We start with the recorded severance deed or the deed by which you acquired the interest, trace forward through any subsequent transfers, and confirm exactly what bundle of rights you hold, full mineral estate, royalty-only, or something narrower, before discussing value. That confirmation protects you from underselling a broader interest than you realize you have, and from overestimating one that's narrower than the family understood.

faqs.q: What's the difference between mineral rights and surface rights?
faqs.a: The surface estate covers the land itself for farming, building and use. The mineral estate covers the oil, gas, coal and other substances beneath it. In West Virginia these are frequently severed and owned separately.

faqs.q: How do I know if my deed conveys full mineral rights or something narrower?
faqs.a: The granting and reservation language in the deed controls. We read the actual document rather than relying on a general label, since older deeds especially can limit the grant by substance or depth.

faqs.q: Do I own the minerals if I only own the surface land?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. If the mineral estate was severed at some point in the property's history, the surface owner and mineral owner can be different people entirely, even generations apart.

faqs.q: Can an operator drill on my land if I only own the minerals, not the surface?
faqs.a: Generally yes, West Virginia law treats the mineral estate as dominant for reasonable development purposes, though the operator typically owes the surface owner compensation for damages under state surface protection provisions.

faqs.q: How do I find my original severance deed?
faqs.a: It's recorded at the county clerk's office in the county where the property sits. If you don't have a copy, we can pull it as part of confirming your title before making an offer.

faqs.q: Can mineral rights be sold separately from surface rights?
faqs.a: Yes, once severed, the mineral estate is its own transferable property right and can be sold, leased or inherited independently of whatever happens to the surface land above it.

faqs.q: What's recorded on a division order versus a mineral deed?
faqs.a: A mineral deed transfers ownership of the interest itself and is recorded at the county clerk's office. A division order is the operator's internal record of your ownership percentage used to calculate royalty payments, and it should match the deed.

image.alt: Mineral Rights mineral rights

items.name: Royalty Interests
items.meta: Own a royalty interest tied to a producing West Virginia well? We confirm your decimal share against the division order and buy the interest directly.

sections.html:
A royalty interest pays you a fraction of production revenue for as long as a lease survives, and the exact fraction is set by a decimal figure that took work to arrive at correctly the first time.

A royalty interest is the right to receive a share of oil and gas production revenue, free of the costs of drilling and operating the well, in exchange for the lease of the underlying mineral rights. In West Virginia, a royalty interest usually arises when a mineral owner leases their acreage to an operator and retains a royalty share as specified in the lease, commonly one-eighth for older agreements, higher for many modern leases signed during and after the Marcellus boom.

Whether that royalty is currently paying out, and how much, depends on the decimal interest calculated by the operator's division order department, a figure that reflects your specific acreage's share of the producing unit and can be worth checking against your own records.

sections.title: How your decimal interest gets calculated
sections.html:
Your royalty decimal is generally your net mineral acres divided by the total unit acreage, multiplied by your lease's royalty fraction. For a tract pooled into a large horizontal unit, that decimal can be quite small even for a meaningful acreage position, since the unit spans many separate tracts. We check this calculation against your division order and your recorded lease to confirm the operator's math matches what your ownership actually supports, since errors do happen, particularly on tracts with a complicated ownership history.

If your acreage was split among heirs after the lease was originally signed, we also confirm that each heir's proportional share of the royalty decimal correctly reflects their fractional ownership, since the operator's records don't always update automatically after a transfer.

sections.title: Flat-rate versus percentage royalty leases
sections.html:
West Virginia has more surviving flat-rate leases than most surrounding states, older agreements that paid a fixed annual sum regardless of actual production volume rather than a percentage royalty. State law has pushed these toward a statutory minimum royalty, with 2018 amendments specifically addressing horizontal wells, but whether your specific lease was properly converted is a factual question we check against the recorded lease date and language before valuing the interest.

An unconverted flat-rate lease and a properly converted percentage lease on otherwise identical acreage are different assets, and we price that distinction directly rather than assuming conversion happened automatically.

sections.title: Why royalty income declines and what that means for value
sections.html: Production from a shale well typically peaks in its first year or two, then declines steadily for the remainder of the well's producing life. This decline curve means a royalty interest's total future value is front-loaded, and the interest is generally worth less per dollar of current royalty income the further the well is past its peak production. We look at your specific well or unit's production history and decline trend, where available through state production records, rather than valuing purely off your most recent check.

sections.title: Documents that let us confirm and price your royalty accurately
sections.html: The most useful documents are your recorded lease, a recent division order, and two or three months of royalty statements showing volumes and prices. With those we can confirm your decimal, check whether the lease terms are being honored correctly, and price the interest against the well's actual production trend rather than a single month's payment.

faqs.q: How do I know if my royalty decimal is correct?
faqs.a: We compare your division order decimal against your net mineral acreage, the unit's total acreage, and your lease's royalty fraction. Discrepancies do turn up, especially on tracts split among multiple heirs.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a flat-rate lease and a percentage royalty lease?
faqs.a: A flat-rate lease pays a fixed annual amount regardless of production volume, common in older West Virginia agreements. A percentage lease pays a share of actual production revenue. State law has pushed flat-rate leases toward a statutory minimum, but we check whether your specific lease was properly converted.

faqs.q: Why has my royalty check gotten smaller over the past couple of years?
faqs.a: Shale wells typically decline in production after their first year or two of peak output, which reduces royalty payments over time even with no change to your lease terms or decimal share.

faqs.q: Do you buy royalty interests that are already producing?
faqs.a: Yes, this is one of the more common interests we buy. We use your division order and recent royalty statements to confirm your decimal and value the interest against the well's actual production trend.

faqs.q: Can I sell just part of my royalty interest and keep the rest?
faqs.a: In some cases yes, depending on how the interest is structured. We can discuss a partial sale if you want to convert some income to cash now while retaining a continued royalty stream.

faqs.q: Do all my siblings need to agree before I sell my share of a family royalty interest?
faqs.a: No. Each heir generally holds their own undivided fractional royalty share and can decide independently, unless a specific agreement among the family says otherwise.

image.alt: Royalty Interests mineral rights

items.name: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI)
items.meta: Own an NPRI in West Virginia, royalty income but no say in leasing? We confirm the reservation language in your deed and buy the interest directly.

sections.html:
A non-participating royalty interest pays you from production but gives you no seat at the table when the mineral owner negotiates the lease, and that split is written into a specific reservation clause somewhere in your family's deed history.

A non-participating royalty interest, usually shortened to NPRI, entitles the holder to a fractional share of production revenue without any right to negotiate leases, receive bonus payments, or participate in decisions about whether and when to drill. In West Virginia, NPRIs typically originate from a deed where a prior owner sold or conveyed the surface and mineral estate but reserved a royalty share for themselves or their heirs, or conversely where a mineral owner sold the executive rights while keeping a royalty carve-out.

Because an NPRI is a fixed, contractual right tied to whatever lease terms the executive rights holder negotiates, its value depends heavily on the reservation language itself, not only on current production.

sections.title: How the reservation clause controls what you're owed
sections.html:
The specific wording that created your NPRI matters enormously. Some reservations specify a fixed royalty fraction, commonly one-eighth or one-sixteenth, regardless of what royalty rate the mineral owner later negotiates in an actual lease. Others are proportionate, entitling the NPRI holder to a set share of whatever royalty the lease specifies. These produce very different payments on the same tract if the underlying lease carries a royalty rate above or below the historical one-eighth standard common in older West Virginia agreements.

We read the original reservation deed carefully before valuing an NPRI, since two interests that look identical on paper can pay very differently depending on this distinction.

sections.title: Why NPRI owners have no leasing control
sections.html:
Unlike a full mineral owner, an NPRI holder can't sign a lease, negotiate a bonus, or block a lease the executive rights holder decides to sign. This means your royalty income depends entirely on decisions made by someone else, whoever holds the executive mineral rights on your tract, including their choice of operator, timing, and negotiated royalty rate. If that party has been slow to lease, or leased on unfavorable terms, an NPRI holder has essentially no recourse beyond whatever protections exist for waste or bad faith dealing.

This dependency is part of why NPRI interests trade differently than full mineral interests, and we factor it directly into any valuation.

sections.title: Confirming your NPRI is still valid and hasn't lapsed
sections.html: Some older West Virginia NPRIs were created with a term limitation, tied to a specific lease or a stated number of years, rather than as a perpetual interest. We check whether your reservation is perpetual or term-limited, and if term-limited, whether it's still within its valid period, before assuming the interest carries ongoing value. A lapsed term NPRI is a materially different asset than a perpetual one even if the original deed language looks similar at a glance.

sections.title: What we need to value and buy your NPRI
sections.html: We want the original reservation deed creating the interest, any subsequent transfer if the NPRI itself changed hands, and your recent royalty statements if the tract is currently producing. From those documents we confirm your fractional share, the fixed-versus-proportionate structure, and whether the interest is perpetual, then put together an offer that reflects the specific mechanics of your reservation rather than a generic royalty estimate.

faqs.q: What makes an NPRI different from owning mineral rights outright?
faqs.a: An NPRI holder receives a royalty share of production but has no right to sign leases, negotiate bonus payments, or make development decisions. Those rights belong to whoever holds the executive mineral interest.

faqs.q: Do I get paid the same royalty rate as the mineral owner's lease?
faqs.a: It depends on how your reservation deed was written. Some NPRIs specify a fixed royalty fraction regardless of the lease's actual rate; others are proportionate to whatever the lease specifies. We check your specific deed language.

faqs.q: Can the mineral owner lease my tract without telling me?
faqs.a: Generally yes, since NPRI holders don't have executive rights. You're typically not a required party to the lease negotiation, though you should still receive your royalty share once production begins.

faqs.q: Is my NPRI perpetual or could it expire?
faqs.a: Some older West Virginia NPRIs were created with term limits tied to a specific lease or a stated number of years. We check the original deed to confirm whether yours is perpetual or term-limited before valuing it.

faqs.q: Can you buy my NPRI even though I don't control the leasing?
faqs.a: Yes. We regularly buy non-participating royalty interests. The lack of executive control is factored into the valuation, but the interest itself is a real, transferable property right.

faqs.q: How is an NPRI different from a working interest?
faqs.a: An NPRI receives royalty income without any cost exposure or leasing authority. A working interest carries both drilling and operating cost exposure and, typically, executive rights. They're valued using entirely different methods.

faqs.q: Can an NPRI be split among multiple heirs like a mineral interest?
faqs.a: Yes. An NPRI is a transferable property right and can be divided through inheritance the same way mineral or royalty interests are, which is common on older West Virginia reservations passed through several generations.

image.alt: Non-Participating Royalty (NPRI) mineral rights

items.name: Surface vs. Mineral Estate
items.meta: Own the surface but not the minerals under your West Virginia land, or the reverse? We trace the severance deed that split the two estates apart.

sections.html:
In West Virginia, owning the land and owning what's beneath it are frequently two entirely separate legal questions, and the deed that split them apart is often older than anyone living on the property today.

Severed mineral estates are widespread across West Virginia, a legacy of coal, timber and land companies buying up mineral and timber rights across the state in the late 1800s and early 1900s while selling or leaving the surface with local farming families. That severance created two distinct, separately transferable estates on the same tract, the surface estate covering the land itself, and the mineral estate covering the oil, gas, coal and other substances beneath it. A century of subsequent transfers, inheritances and family sales has often sent those two estates in completely different directions.

Whether you own just the surface, just the minerals, or both, understanding which one you hold, and what that means for the other, starts with tracing the original severance deed.

sections.title: Finding the deed that split the estates
sections.html:
The severance usually happened through a specific recorded deed, sometimes labeled a mineral deed or a reservation within a broader land sale, where a prior owner sold the surface but reserved the minerals, or sold the minerals while keeping the surface. That deed's date and exact language control what was actually severed, all minerals, specific substances like coal or oil and gas, or a limited depth range. We trace this document at the county clerk's office as the starting point for confirming what estate you currently hold.

In many West Virginia counties this severance dates to between 1890 and 1920, tied to the coal and timber boom of that era, well before anyone anticipated horizontal shale drilling would make the mineral estate valuable again generations later.

sections.title: What surface owners are entitled to when minerals are developed
sections.html: If you own the surface but not the minerals, West Virginia's oil and gas surface owner protections generally require an operator to provide notice before entering to drill and to compensate you for damages to the surface, crops, fencing and other improvements caused by development, even though the mineral estate is legally dominant for reasonable development purposes. Surface owners don't typically share in royalty income unless they separately hold some mineral or royalty interest, but the compensation and notice protections are worth understanding if development activity is moving into your area.

sections.title: What mineral owners without surface rights should know
sections.html: If you own minerals but not the surface, you generally don't need the surface owner's permission to lease those minerals or to have an operator access the land for reasonable development, though the operator typically owes the surface owner compensation independent of your royalty. This dominant-estate structure is part of what makes a severed mineral interest valuable and sellable on its own, separate from any relationship with whoever currently farms or lives on the surface above it.

sections.title: Confirming which estate, or both, you actually hold
sections.html: Some West Virginia families still hold both the surface and the minerals on ancestral land, never severed by an earlier generation. Others hold one or the other, sometimes without fully realizing which. We trace the recorded deed history to confirm exactly what estate, or estates, you own before discussing any sale, since surface and mineral interests are valued through entirely different lenses and a sale of one has no bearing on ownership of the other.

faqs.q: How do I know if my mineral rights were severed from my surface land?
faqs.a: Check your deed and the recorded chain behind it at the county clerk's office. A severance deed, sometimes labeled a mineral deed or a reservation clause within a land sale, is what would have split the two estates apart.

faqs.q: I own the surface. Do I get any royalty if a well is drilled?
faqs.a: Not unless you separately hold a mineral or royalty interest. Surface ownership alone generally doesn't entitle you to production royalties, though you're entitled to notice and compensation for surface damages under West Virginia's surface owner protections.

faqs.q: Can an operator drill without the surface owner's permission?
faqs.a: Generally yes, if the mineral estate is validly severed and leased, since West Virginia treats the mineral estate as dominant for reasonable development, subject to the operator's obligation to compensate the surface owner for damages.

faqs.q: Can I sell my mineral rights without the surface owner's involvement?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. A severed mineral estate is its own separately transferable property right and doesn't require the surface owner's consent or participation to sell.

faqs.q: My family still owns both the surface and the minerals. Does that change anything?
faqs.a: It can simplify some things, since there's no separate surface owner to coordinate with on access or damages, but the mineral and surface portions are still valued and can be sold separately if you decide to sell only one.

faqs.q: Does selling my mineral rights affect my ownership of the surface land?
faqs.a: No. Selling a severed mineral interest doesn't touch surface ownership at all, since the two estates are legally separate once severed. You keep the surface land exactly as before.

image.alt: Surface vs. Mineral Estate mineral rights

items.name: Overriding Royalty Interests (ORRI)
items.meta: Hold an ORRI carved out of a West Virginia oil and gas lease? We trace the assignment that created it and confirm the lease is still active before making an offer.

sections.html:
An overriding royalty interest lives and dies with a specific lease, and confirming that lease is still in effect is the first thing we check before valuing one.

An overriding royalty interest, or ORRI, is a share of production carved out of a specific oil and gas lease rather than out of the mineral estate itself. It's most often created when a landman, geologist or small operator assigns a lease to a larger operator but retains a royalty percentage as part of the deal, or when an original leaseholder sells the working interest while keeping an override for themselves. In West Virginia, ORRIs from the early Marcellus land rush are common, since a lot of leasehold changed hands multiple times between the original land agent and the company that eventually drilled the well.

Because an ORRI exists only as long as the underlying lease does, tracing that lease's status is the whole ballgame before we can value the interest.

sections.title: Why an ORRI depends entirely on the lease surviving
sections.html:
Unlike a mineral or royalty interest tied to the land itself, an ORRI terminates automatically if the underlying lease expires or is released, since there's nothing left for the override to attach to. This makes lease status the central question for any ORRI valuation. A tract held by production with an active, producing well supports an ORRI with real ongoing value. A tract where the underlying lease lapsed years ago means the override lapsed right along with it, regardless of what the original assignment document said.

We pull the recorded lease and any release or extension documents at the county clerk's office to confirm current status before assuming your ORRI still has value.

sections.title: Tracing the assignment that created your override
sections.html:
The assignment document that carved out your ORRI specifies the exact percentage and often the specific lease or leases it applies to. In West Virginia's Marcellus counties, leasehold assignments during the early development years sometimes covered large blocks of acreage, meaning your override might apply across multiple wells within a broader area rather than a single tract. We read the assignment carefully to confirm the scope, since an ORRI covering an entire block pays differently than one limited to a single well.

If the assignment has itself been transferred since it was created, which happens when an ORRI holder sells or passes the interest to heirs, we also trace that subsequent chain to confirm current ownership, checking each recorded assignment against the county clerk's index.

sections.title: How ORRI value compares to a straight royalty interest
sections.html: An ORRI and a mineral or royalty interest in the same tract can produce similar-looking royalty checks while carrying very different underlying risk. The ORRI's dependence on lease survival, combined with the fact that it often applies to a specific well or defined area rather than the broader mineral estate, generally makes it a narrower, more concentrated bet on that lease's continued production than owning the minerals themselves would be. We price that difference explicitly rather than treating an ORRI and a mineral royalty as interchangeable.

sections.title: Documents that let us move quickly on an ORRI purchase
sections.html: We want the original assignment document creating your override, the underlying lease it attaches to, and your recent royalty statements if the interest is producing. If the ORRI passed to you through inheritance, we'll also need whatever probate or estate documentation established your current ownership before we can close.

faqs.q: What happens to my ORRI if the underlying lease expires?
faqs.a: It terminates along with the lease, since an override only exists as a carve-out from that specific lease's production. This is why confirming the lease is still active is the first step in valuing an ORRI.

faqs.q: How is an ORRI different from a mineral royalty interest?
faqs.a: An ORRI is carved out of a specific lease and disappears if that lease ends. A mineral or NPRI royalty interest is tied to the land itself and survives even if a particular lease is released and a new one is signed later.

faqs.q: My ORRI came from an assignment my father signed decades ago. Is it still valid?
faqs.a: It depends on whether the underlying lease is still active, held by production or otherwise in effect. We trace the recorded lease and assignment history to confirm current status before making an offer.

faqs.q: Does my override apply to just one well or a larger area?
faqs.a: That depends on the scope described in the original assignment document, which sometimes covered a defined tract and sometimes a broader leasehold block. We read the assignment to confirm exactly what your override covers.

faqs.q: Can you buy an ORRI I inherited?
faqs.a: Yes, provided we can confirm your ownership through probate or estate documentation and confirm the underlying lease is still active. We'll walk through exactly what's needed once we see your paperwork.

faqs.q: Is an ORRI riskier to hold than a mineral royalty interest?
faqs.a: Generally yes, because its entire value depends on one specific lease surviving, rather than the broader mineral estate, which continues to exist even if a lease lapses and gets replaced with a new one later.

image.alt: Overriding Royalty Interests (ORRI) mineral rights

items.name: Working Interests
items.meta: Hold a working interest with West Virginia drilling and operating cost exposure? We confirm the operating agreement and joint interest billing before buying.

sections.html:
A working interest is the one mineral asset in West Virginia where you're on the hook for costs as well as entitled to revenue, and that changes the whole conversation compared to a royalty.

A working interest gives the holder the right to explore for and produce oil and gas, but also carries a proportionate share of the costs of drilling, completing and operating the well, unlike a royalty interest, which is free of those costs. In West Virginia, working interests most often show up with small legacy owners, individuals or families who participated financially in an older vertical well, sometimes decades ago, in the Big Injun, Gordon or another shallow sand, and still hold a fractional working interest subject to ongoing joint interest billing from the operator.

Because a working interest comes with both upside and cost exposure, valuing one requires looking at the operating agreement and recent billing history, not merely a royalty check.

sections.title: Why working interests carry cost exposure a royalty doesn't
sections.html:
A working interest owner is billed their proportionate share of operating expenses, workovers, and any capital costs the operator incurs on the well or unit, deducted against their share of production revenue rather than paid separately. On an older, marginal well past its productive peak, operating costs can approach or even exceed revenue in a slow month, meaning a small working interest can occasionally generate a net bill rather than a net payment. This is the central risk that distinguishes a working interest from every other mineral interest type, and it's the first thing we evaluate.

We ask for recent joint interest billing statements alongside any revenue statements to see the real net picture before valuing your interest.

sections.title: Reading the operating agreement itself
sections.html:
The joint operating agreement governing your well specifies how costs are allocated, what happens if a working interest owner doesn't pay their share, and whether there are any preferential rights or consent requirements attached to a transfer of the interest. Some older West Virginia operating agreements include a right of first refusal for other working interest owners in the unit, which can affect how a sale needs to be structured and who needs to be notified before closing.

We review this agreement specifically, since working interest transfers sometimes require more coordination with the operator or other owners than a straightforward mineral or royalty sale would.

sections.title: Legacy vertical well working interests versus modern horizontal units
sections.html: Most working interests we see in West Virginia trace back to small, local participation in shallow vertical wells drilled before the horizontal shale era, often a modest cash investment made by a family decades ago in exchange for a small percentage working interest. These wells are typically well past peak production now, which means the cost-versus-revenue balance matters more than it would have in the well's early years. We look at recent production and cost trends for the specific well, not general county activity, since working interest value is tied tightly to that individual well's current economics.

sections.title: What we need to evaluate a working interest
sections.html: We want the joint operating agreement, your assignment or participation document establishing the interest, and at least six months of joint interest billing and revenue statements. That billing history is the single most useful document for a working interest, since it shows the actual net economics rather than a gross revenue figure that doesn't account for your cost exposure.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a working interest and a royalty interest?
faqs.a: A working interest carries a proportionate share of drilling and operating costs along with production revenue. A royalty interest receives revenue free of those costs. Working interests carry more risk and require more paperwork to evaluate.

faqs.q: Can a working interest actually lose money in a given month?
faqs.a: Yes, particularly on an older, marginal well where operating costs and any workover expenses can approach or exceed that month's revenue share. This is why we review joint interest billing history rather than valuing off a single payment.

faqs.q: Do I need the other working interest owners' permission to sell mine?
faqs.a: Sometimes. Some joint operating agreements include a right of first refusal for other owners in the unit. We check your specific agreement to confirm what's required before closing.

faqs.q: My working interest comes from an old vertical well my grandfather invested in. Is it still worth anything?
faqs.a: Possibly, depending on the well's current production and cost trend. Many legacy shallow wells are past peak production, so we look closely at recent billing and revenue statements to determine real current value.

faqs.q: What documents speed up a working interest sale?
faqs.a: The joint operating agreement, the assignment or participation document establishing your interest, and at least six months of joint interest billing statements are the most useful starting point.

faqs.q: Does selling a working interest transfer my cost exposure to the buyer?
faqs.a: Yes. Once the sale closes and the assignment is recorded, future drilling and operating costs, along with future revenue, become the buyer's responsibility, not yours, going forward.

items.name: Marcellus Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: West Virginia Marcellus owners in Doddridge, Harrison, Marshall, Wetzel and Tyler counties: get your abstract reviewed and a benchmarked offer before you sign anything.

sections.html:
Every Marcellus tract in West Virginia carries a paper trail, and the value of your interest is usually written into that trail before a single royalty check confirms it.

The Marcellus in West Virginia runs through the north-central counties in a band that includes Doddridge, Harrison, Marshall, Wetzel, Tyler, Ritchie and parts of Monongalia and Marion. Horizontal development took off there around 2008 and 2009, but most of the mineral estates underneath those laterals were severed decades earlier, often through coal or timber company deeds from the early 1900s that carved the surface away from the oil, gas and coal beneath it.

That gap between the drilling date and the severance date is where most title problems live. Before we quote anything on a Marcellus interest, we pull the deed and lease chain at the county clerk's office and compare it against whatever operator division order paperwork you're holding. A number without a title check behind it is a guess, not an offer.

sections.title: Where the play sits and what it means for your tract
sections.html:
The Marcellus in this part of West Virginia sits roughly 4,000 to 8,500 feet down, thickening toward the Pennsylvania line and thinning as you move south and west out of the core counties. Laterals run one to two miles, and a single well now typically drains a unit assembled from dozens of separate tracts, which means your royalty decimal is often a small slice of a large pooled unit rather than a clean fraction of your original acreage.

Operators active in the West Virginia Marcellus have shifted over the years, with EQT, Antero Resources, Northeast Natural Energy and Southwestern's successor entities holding the bulk of current production. Older leases from the 2008-2011 land rush were frequently assigned two or three times before a well was ever permitted, so the party paying your royalty today is rarely the party whose landman knocked on the door.

sections.title: Legacy vertical wells layered under the horizontal program
sections.html:
A lot of West Virginia Marcellus tracts already had shallow vertical wells producing out of the Big Injun, Gordon or Fifth Sand before the horizontal boom arrived. Those older leases sometimes cover only the shallow rights, or they cover 'oil and gas' broadly and got swept into the deeper Marcellus unit by their own habendum clause. Sorting out whether your shallow lease actually reaches the Marcellus, or whether a separate deep-rights lease was signed later, changes what you own and what a buyer will pay for it.

We see this most often on tracts where a family kept a small stripper well running for personal use or minimal royalty for thirty years, then discovered the same acreage sat inside a new horizontal unit with a different operator and a different decimal entirely.

sections.title: Flat-rate leases and the conversion that changed West Virginia royalties
sections.html:
West Virginia has more surviving flat-rate leases than almost any other Appalachian state, agreements written before the 1982 statutory minimum that paid a flat annual sum, sometimes a few hundred dollars, instead of a percentage of production. State law has since pushed those leases toward a minimum one-eighth royalty on gas actually produced, and the 2018 amendments extended that treatment to horizontal Marcellus wells specifically. If your family's lease predates that fix and nobody ever filed the paperwork to convert it, you may be owed more than the operator is currently paying, and that unresolved conversion issue also affects what your interest is worth to a buyer.

We check the recorded lease date and royalty clause against the conversion statute before we value a flat-rate tract, because an unconverted flat-rate lease and a properly converted one are not the same asset even if the acreage is identical.

sections.title: Heirship and fractional interests inside Marcellus units
sections.html: Because so much West Virginia mineral ownership passed down through generations without formal probate, a single Marcellus royalty check is often split among a dozen or more heirs holding fractional undivided interests, some as small as a few hundredths of one percent. The state's Co-Tenancy Modernization and Majority Protection Act lets a majority of the identified owners lease or participate on behalf of unlocated or nonconsenting co-tenants for horizontal units, but it doesn't fix the underlying title. If your name only shows up because a great-aunt died intestate in 1974 and nobody ever recorded a settlement, that gap in the chain has to be documented, not guessed at, before a sale can close cleanly.

faqs.q: How is a West Virginia Marcellus royalty different from a flat vertical well royalty?
faqs.a: A horizontal Marcellus unit typically pools many tracts, so your royalty decimal reflects your acreage's share of the whole unit rather than the well sitting on your land specifically. Two neighboring owners can have very different decimals depending on when they signed and how the unit was drawn.

faqs.q: What if my family's lease is one of the old flat-rate agreements?
faqs.a: We pull the recorded lease and check the royalty clause against West Virginia's conversion statute. Depending on the lease date and whether the well is horizontal, you may be entitled to the statutory minimum royalty going forward, which we factor into any offer we make.

faqs.q: Do I need to sort out heirship before I can sell?
faqs.a: Not always before we make an offer, but it has to be resolved before closing. We can often work from the recorded probate or intestate succession records at the county clerk's office and tell you early what documentation the closing will require.

faqs.q: Can you tell me what my Marcellus interest is worth without seeing my lease?
faqs.a: Not accurately. Values vary with the unit's decimal, the operator's current activity, recent royalty statements and whether the lease is flat-rate or percentage. We ask for a copy of your last division order or royalty check to start a real conversation.

faqs.q: Why does the operator on my check keep changing?
faqs.a: Marcellus leasehold in West Virginia has been assigned and sold repeatedly since the original land rush. The operating company can change without any change to your underlying lease terms, though it's worth confirming the assignment was properly recorded at the courthouse.

items.name: Utica Shale Mineral Rights
items.meta: Utica and Point Pleasant rights under West Virginia's northern panhandle sit beneath the Marcellus lease. We check which zones your deed and lease actually cover.

sections.html:
In the northern panhandle, the Utica and Point Pleasant sit two thousand feet or more below the Marcellus, and whether your paperwork reaches that deep is a title question, not a geology question.

The Utica Shale and the underlying Point Pleasant limestone are best known as an Ohio play, but the formation extends across the state line into West Virginia's northern panhandle counties, principally Marshall, Wetzel, Tyler and Doddridge. Development there has been slower and more selective than in Ohio, with operators drilling deep Utica tests as a secondary target beneath acreage already held by Marcellus production.

Because most West Virginia panhandle tracts were leased for Marcellus first, the question we work through with owners is whether that same lease's granting clause reaches the deeper Utica and Point Pleasant zones, or whether a separate deep-rights lease is needed before anyone can drill or pay you on that horizon.

sections.title: A deeper target stacked under existing Marcellus leasehold
sections.html:
Most West Virginia Utica activity has come from operators who already held Marcellus rights in Marshall and Wetzel counties and tested the deeper section from existing pad locations. Point Pleasant depths in the panhandle run well past 10,000 feet, meaningfully deeper and more expensive to drill than the overlying Marcellus, which is part of why development has stayed concentrated in a narrow band rather than spreading county-wide the way Marcellus drilling did.

For an owner, that means a tract can carry an active, producing Marcellus lease while the Utica underneath it remains entirely unleased or covered by a lease whose depth language is ambiguous. We read the granting clause specifically for 'all depths' or 'all formations' language versus a depth-limited grant before assuming the two zones are tied together.

sections.title: Older leases and depth severance in the panhandle
sections.html:
Some panhandle leases signed during the early Marcellus rush were drafted with narrower depth language than became standard later, occasionally limiting the grant to a specific formation or a stated depth. If your family's original lease predates 2010, it's worth confirming what depths it actually covers before assuming a Utica test on the same pad automatically pays you under the same terms as the Marcellus.

We've also seen tracts where the mineral estate itself was severed by depth generations ago, coal-era deeds sometimes carved out oil and gas to a stated depth rather than the full mineral column, which is a separate issue from lease coverage and has to be traced through the recorded chain of title at the county clerk's office.

sections.title: What Point Pleasant activity does to fractional interest value
sections.html:
Where operators have confirmed productive Point Pleasant results near your tract, that changes how a buyer thinks about acreage that otherwise looks unremarkable on the surface. Even a small, fractional interest inherited through several generations of heirs can carry meaningfully different value depending on whether it sits inside a Marshall or Wetzel County unit with confirmed deep results versus acreage further south or west where no Utica test has been drilled nearby.

We price against recent activity and recorded permits in your specific unit rather than county-wide averages, because Utica development in West Virginia is concentrated enough that being a few miles outside the active band matters.

sections.title: Confirming what you actually own before any offer
sections.html: Before we quote a West Virginia Utica or Point Pleasant interest, we want the original severance deed if it's available, the current lease if one exists, and your most recent division order or royalty statement. That combination tells us whether you're dealing with a full mineral estate, a depth-limited interest, or a small undivided fraction split among heirs, and each of those changes the number.

faqs.q: Is the Utica the same lease as my Marcellus lease?
faqs.a: Not necessarily. It depends on the granting clause in your original lease. Some cover all depths and formations, others were written narrower. We check the recorded lease language before assuming both zones are covered.

faqs.q: Where in West Virginia is Utica activity actually happening?
faqs.a: Development has been concentrated in the northern panhandle, primarily Marshall, Wetzel and parts of Tyler and Doddridge counties, generally from pads that already hold Marcellus production. Activity outside that band has been limited.

faqs.q: My mineral rights are unleased for the Utica but leased for the Marcellus. Can I still sell?
faqs.a: Yes. We can value the leased Marcellus interest and the unleased deeper rights separately, since they carry different risk and timeline until a buyer or operator confirms what's underneath.

faqs.q: How deep is the Point Pleasant in the panhandle?
faqs.a: It typically runs past 10,000 feet in the areas being tested, considerably deeper than the overlying Marcellus, which is one reason drilling costs and pace have differed between the two zones.

faqs.q: What documents speed up a Utica interest sale?
faqs.a: Your original severance deed if you have it, any lease covering the tract, and a recent division order or royalty statement showing the current operator and decimal. Those let us confirm depth coverage without a slow courthouse search on our side alone.

items.name: How to Sell Mineral Rights
items.meta: A step-by-step look at how a West Virginia mineral rights sale actually proceeds, from title review through closing and recording.

sections.html:
Selling a mineral interest in West Virginia follows a fairly consistent sequence, even when the tract itself has an unusual title history, and knowing the sequence in advance removes most of the surprise.

Owners who have never sold a mineral interest before often expect the process to resemble a real estate closing, and in some ways it does, but the title work behind a mineral sale tends to run deeper because West Virginia mineral estates are so frequently severed, fractionalized among heirs, or tied up in old flat-rate leases from a different era of drilling. Understanding the actual steps ahead of time makes the process far less opaque.

Below is the typical sequence for a West Virginia mineral sale, from the first conversation about your interest through the recorded deed that finalizes the transfer.

sections.title: Step one: identify what you actually own
sections.html: Before any valuation conversation makes sense, you need clarity on your net mineral acreage, whether the interest is leased or unleased, producing or non-producing, and whether you own it outright or as one of several heirs holding an undivided interest. This is where your deed, any prior lease, and estate records come into play. A buyer will ask these questions early, and having answers ready speeds everything that follows.

sections.title: Step two: preliminary title review
sections.html:
A serious buyer will run at least a preliminary check of the recorded chain of title in the county where your minerals sit, tracing ownership back through the severance deed and any subsequent transfers or estates. In West Virginia this step frequently surfaces one of a few recurring issues: an unprobated estate somewhere in the chain, a fractional share that was never formally distributed among siblings, or a decades-old flat-rate lease that is still technically in effect and needs to be accounted for in the offer.

None of these issues are unusual, and none of them typically stop a sale. They do determine how the offer is structured and what curative paperwork, if any, needs to be signed alongside the deed.

sections.title: Step three: the offer and purchase agreement
sections.html:
Once your ownership picture is clear, a buyer will put together an offer reflecting your net mineral acreage, lease status, and any production history, and present a purchase agreement laying out price, closing timeline, and any conditions tied to curing title issues found during review. This is the point to ask questions about how the price was derived and what, if anything, is contingent on further title work.

Offers on producing interests are typically informed by recent royalty statements and the decline behavior of the well; offers on unleased minerals are informed more by leasing activity and lease bonus trends in the surrounding area. Either way, value talk should always be framed as a range tied to current activity rather than a fixed promise, since production and market conditions change.

sections.title: Step four: closing and recording
sections.html:
At closing you sign a mineral deed conveying your interest, which is then recorded in the county clerk's office where the property sits, updating the public record so future title searches reflect the new owner. If your interest is currently leased and producing, the buyer will also typically send notice to the operator so that future royalty payments are redirected under a new division order.

If your sale required curative work, such as an affidavit of heirship or a corrective deed, that document is usually recorded alongside or just ahead of the mineral deed itself, so the chain of title reads cleanly for whoever searches it next.

Keep a copy of your recorded deed for your own records once the sale closes. It is the document that confirms the transfer went through and can be useful later if any question ever arises about the tract or about other interests you may still hold nearby.

faqs.q: How long does a typical mineral sale take in West Virginia?
faqs.a: A clean title with a straightforward chain can close in a few weeks. Sales involving unprobated estates, multiple undivided heirs, or old flat-rate leases that need review typically take longer while the curative paperwork is prepared and recorded.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to sell my mineral rights?
faqs.a: It is not always required, but for interests with a complicated estate history, engaging an attorney familiar with West Virginia mineral title is often worthwhile, particularly if multiple heirs or an unresolved probate are involved.

faqs.q: Can I sell only part of my mineral interest?
faqs.a: Yes. Owners frequently sell a fractional share, a specific depth interval, or just the executive rights while retaining the rest, depending on how the deed is structured.

faqs.q: What happens to my existing lease if I sell?
faqs.a: An existing lease generally stays in place and transfers with the minerals. The buyer becomes the lessor of record and receives future royalty payments under a new division order once the operator is notified of the sale.

faqs.q: What if my interest is held in an estate that is still open?
faqs.a: A sale can often proceed with the executor or administrator signing on behalf of the estate, or after distribution to heirs, depending on how far along probate is. This is worth raising early with whoever is handling the sale so the closing timeline accounts for it.

items.name: What Are Mineral Rights Worth?
items.meta: What actually drives the value of West Virginia mineral rights, from production history and play position to title clarity and lease terms.

sections.html:
Value in a West Virginia mineral interest comes from a handful of factors that a title examiner and a buyer both look at, and none of them is a single number you can look up.

It is a reasonable question with an unsatisfying honest answer: what your mineral interest is worth depends on where it sits, what is currently happening on it, and how clean its title chain is, and any of those can shift the number substantially. Rather than offer a shortcut, this guide walks through the factors that actually move value, so you can look at your own tract with a clearer eye.

The goal here is not to give you a dollar figure, since anyone offering one without seeing your production history and title records is guessing. The goal is to help you understand what a buyer is actually weighing.

sections.title: Producing versus non-producing
sections.html:
A producing interest has an actual income stream to model, which generally makes it more straightforward to value than acreage with no current production, since royalty statements provide a real basis for projecting future decline. Non-producing minerals, whether leased and awaiting drilling or entirely unleased, are valued more speculatively, based on nearby drilling activity, comparable lease terms, and how likely the tract is to be developed in a reasonable timeframe.

Within producing interests, where the well sits on its decline curve matters as much as current volume. A well several years into production behaves very differently going forward than one still in its early, higher-volume period, and a title researcher pulling several years of statements can usually tell which phase a given well is in just from the shape of the volume trend.

sections.title: Play position and formation
sections.html: West Virginia acreage sitting in the core of an active play generally attracts more attention and stronger comparable lease and sale activity than acreage on the flank, farther from concentrated recent drilling. This is not a fixed geographic line and shifts over time as operators focus development in different areas, which is part of why recent, local comparable data matters more than general assumptions about a county.

sections.title: Lease terms already in place
sections.html:
An interest already leased under strong, current royalty terms is generally viewed differently than the same acreage sitting under an old flat-rate lease that pays a fixed sum regardless of production, or under no lease at all. A flat-rate lease in particular can suppress near-term income well below what the acreage would produce under a modern royalty structure, and any honest valuation of that interest has to account for the gap between what the lease currently pays and what the underlying production or leasing environment would otherwise support.

West Virginia has enough of these older flat-rate arrangements still on the books that a title researcher working through a county's records will run across them regularly, often on tracts that have not seen a new lease negotiated in decades even while nearby acreage has been actively developed under modern terms.

sections.title: Title clarity
sections.html:
An interest with a clean, current, recorded chain of title values more predictably and closes faster than one sitting behind an unresolved estate, an undivided interest split among heirs who have never formally documented their shares, or a decades-old deed with an ambiguous legal description. This does not mean a messy title chain makes an interest worthless, only that it typically adds time and curative steps before a buyer can finalize an offer with confidence.

In practice, this is one of the more overlooked levers an owner actually controls. Production trends and play position are largely out of your hands, but pulling together your deed, estate records, and any missing heirship documentation before you start a sale conversation puts you in the strongest possible position when an offer is finally put together.

faqs.q: Is there a standard price per acre for West Virginia minerals?
faqs.a: No. Values vary widely depending on play position, production status, lease terms, and title clarity, and any figure quoted without reviewing your specific tract and history should be treated as a rough range at best.

faqs.q: Does an old flat-rate lease reduce what I can get for my minerals?
faqs.a: It can reduce near-term royalty income, but a buyer evaluating the underlying interest will typically account for the difference between what the flat-rate lease currently pays and the acreage's broader production or leasing potential.

faqs.q: Will an unresolved estate lower my offer?
faqs.a: It usually does not lower the underlying value of the interest itself, but it can extend the time and paperwork needed to close, and a buyer will factor that timeline into how an offer is structured.

faqs.q: Should I get my minerals valued before or after I resolve heirship issues?
faqs.a: Either can work, since a preliminary conversation about value does not require resolved title, but any final offer will depend on the title work being completed, so starting that process early generally speeds things up.

faqs.q: Can two adjoining tracts in the same county have very different values?
faqs.a: Yes, and often significantly so. Differences in spacing unit position, which formations are held by production, existing lease terms, and even which heirs are documented as owners can produce meaningfully different values on tracts that look identical on a map.
